explanations.explanation: The poet says, "How the gold has become tarnished, the pure gold has become dull!" (Lamentations 4:1). Gold is supposed to shine, and this gold has lost it. I think that's why the poem opens with "How," like he can hardly believe what he's looking at. The gold is still there, but its shine is gone.
The poet never mentions melting. He says the pure gold has become tarnished and dull. What he mourns is the lost shine, and I think that's quieter than melting and sadder.

Nobody is hauling the gold away in this verse. The poet says the pure gold has become dull. What he's mourning is the lost shine. The verse adds that the gems of the temple lie scattered on every street corner.

The poet says Zion's precious sons, "…once worth their weight in pure gold, are now esteemed as jars of clay, the work of a potter’s hands!" (Lamentations 4:2). That's a long drop from gold to clay. It's a hard picture of how low they've fallen.

Chaff is a picture the Bible uses in other places, like Psalm 1:4, but it's not the one this poet picks here. He says Zion's precious sons are now esteemed as "…jars of clay, the work of a potter’s hands!" Gold to clay is the drop he's pointing at. Keep your eye on those clay jars.

Grass is a picture the Bible uses elsewhere, like in Isaiah 40:7, but not in this verse. Here the poet says the sons once worth their weight in pure gold are esteemed as "…jars of clay, the work of a potter’s hands!" (Lamentations 4:2). So the picture is a potter's work, not a field. It's gold on one side and clay on the other.

The poet says, "Even jackals offer their breasts to nurse their young, but the daughter of my people has become cruel, like an ostrich in the wilderness." (Lamentations 4:3). A jackal is a wild animal, and even it feeds its young. He's saying his own people have fallen below that. It's a hard thing to say about your own.

Weary sounds close, but it's not the poet's word. He says the daughter of his people "…has become cruel, like an ostrich in the wilderness." He's setting that next to the jackals, who still nurse their young. Cruel is the word that makes that comparison land.

Nothing here is about being fearless. The poet says even jackals nurse their young, "…but the daughter of my people has become cruel, like an ostrich in the wilderness." (Lamentations 4:3). The point is the contrast with the jackals. Fearless wouldn't make the sting.

I think this is the hard one to hear. The poet says, "Little children beg for bread, but no one gives them any." (Lamentations 4:4). Nobody hands them any, so the answer is false. It comes right after the thirsty infant, so the picture gets heavier.

Yes, and it's a heavy one. The poet says, "Little children beg for bread, but no one gives them any." (Lamentations 4:4). They ask, and nobody hands them a thing. He doesn't say why, and I won't guess.

The poet says, "those brought up in crimson huddle in ash heaps." (Lamentations 4:5). Crimson was the color of how they were raised, and now they're in the ashes. The same verse says those who once ate delicacies are destitute in the streets. It's a hard turn from rich color to gray ash.
Caves aren't in this verse. The poet says, "those brought up in crimson huddle in ash heaps." (Lamentations 4:5). Crimson on one side and ashes on the other is the whole picture.

The city gate isn't what the poet names. He says that those brought up in crimson "…huddle in ash heaps." (Lamentations 4:5). They huddle there, and that word makes me picture people pulling in close. The same verse says those who once ate delicacies are destitute in the streets.

The poet says the punishment of the daughter of his people "…is greater than that of Sodom…" Sodom was overthrown in an instant (Lamentations 4:6), and the LORD rained sulfur and fire on it (Genesis 19:24). That's a hard thing to say. I think he's showing how heavy his people's punishment is.

It's the other way around. The poet says the punishment of the daughter of his people "…is greater than that of Sodom, which was overthrown in an instant without a hand turned to help her." (Lamentations 4:6). Sodom is the city the LORD rained sulfur and fire on (Genesis 19:24). He's saying his people's punishment is greater than that.

The poet says, "But now their appearance is blacker than soot; they are not recognized in the streets." (Lamentations 4:8). Before, they were brighter than snow and whiter than milk. Now they're darker than soot. The swing from bright to black is the whole sadness of it.

Gray is a good guess, but the poet goes darker. He says their appearance is "…blacker than soot…" (Lamentations 4:8). Back in verse 7 they were brighter than snow and whiter than milk. Gray would be a soft landing, and he doesn't give them one.

Red does show up, but in the earlier verse. The poet says their bodies were "…more ruddy than rubies…" back when things were good (Lamentations 4:7). Now he says their appearance is "…blacker than soot…" (Lamentations 4:8). That's the change he's mourning.

The poet says the opposite. He says of the dignitaries, "they are not recognized in the streets." (Lamentations 4:8). Their appearance is blacker than soot, and their skin has shriveled on their bones. That's how far they've changed.
The poet says, "they are not recognized in the streets." (Lamentations 4:8). Their appearance is blacker than soot. Their skin has shriveled on their bones and become "…as dry as a stick."

The poet says, "Those slain by the sword are better off than those who die of hunger, who waste away, pierced with pain because the fields lack produce." (Lamentations 4:9). It's a hard line, and I think it shows how slow and awful the hunger is. He says the fields lack produce. That's the pain he's naming.

explanations.answer: Those who hid in the hills
explanations.explanation: Hiding in the hills isn't in this verse. The poet says, "Those slain by the sword are better off than those who die of hunger…" (Lamentations 4:9). The hunger is what he calls worse. It's heavy, so I'll say it plain: it's a hard line to read.

Egypt doesn't come up in this verse. The poet says, "Those slain by the sword are better off than those who die of hunger, who waste away, pierced with pain because the fields lack produce." (Lamentations 4:9). So the ones he compares are those slain by the sword. It's a heavy line, and I think it shows how much the hunger hurts.

The poet says the LORD "…has kindled a fire in Zion, and it has consumed her foundations." (Lamentations 4:11). A foundation is what everything else sits on, so this fire reached deep. This is the end of the first half of the poem.

Palaces would make sense, but that's not the word. The poet says the fire "…has consumed her foundations." (Lamentations 4:11). Foundations are what a whole city is built on, so this is deeper than one grand building.
Vineyards aren't in this verse. The poet says the LORD "…has kindled a fire in Zion, and it has consumed her foundations." (Lamentations 4:11). It's the base of everything, not one field or crop.

The poet says, "…this was for the sins of her prophets and the guilt of her priests, who shed the blood of the righteous in her midst." (Lamentations 4:13). Prophets and priests are the ones he names. He says it plainly and doesn't soften it.

Kings and soldiers aren't who the poet names here. He says "…this was for the sins of her prophets and the guilt of her priests, who shed the blood of the righteous in her midst." (Lamentations 4:13). So it's prophets and priests. I think that's what makes it so heavy.

The elders do show up later in the poem, but not here. In this verse the poet says it was "…for the sins of her prophets and the guilt of her priests, who shed the blood of the righteous in her midst." (Lamentations 4:13). He names prophets and priests. Those are the two he points at.

The men shout, "Go away! Unclean!" and then, "Away, away! Do not touch us!" (Lamentations 4:15). The ones they shout at are wandering blind, defiled by blood. So people won't even touch their garments. It's a lonely picture.

The poet doesn't use that word. The men shout, "Go away! Unclean!" (Lamentations 4:15). It goes with what the verse before says: the people were defiled by blood, and no one dared to touch their garments. Unclean is the word that fits.

Strangers isn't the word. The men shout, "Go away! Unclean!" and "Away, away! Do not touch us!" (Lamentations 4:15). Verse 14 says the people they're shouting at wandered blind, defiled by blood. That's why the cry is unclean.

They aren't welcomed. The poet says, "So they fled and wandered. Among the nations it was said, “They can stay here no longer.”" (Lamentations 4:15). First they're shouted at, and then it's said among the nations that they can stay here no longer. It's a hard road for them.

Right, they're not welcomed. The poet says, "So they fled and wandered. Among the nations it was said, “They can stay here no longer.”" (Lamentations 4:15). They fled and wandered. That's a hard road.

The poet says, "The priests are shown no honor; the elders find no favor." (Lamentations 4:16). The verse begins with the presence of the LORD scattering them. So the honor being gone is part of the same sad picture.
Hiding isn't what the poet says. He says, "The priests are shown no honor; the elders find no favor." (Lamentations 4:16). It's about how people treat them now. The honor is gone.

explanations.answer: They are told to stay silent
explanations.explanation: Nobody tells the priests to be quiet in this verse. The poet says, "The priests are shown no honor; the elders find no favor." (Lamentations 4:16). It's about how they're treated: no honor. And the elders find no favor either.

The poet says the opposite. He says, "We watched from our towers for a nation that could not save us." (Lamentations 4:17). They looked and looked, and their eyes were failing. The help they hoped for couldn't do it.

Right. The poet says, "All the while our eyes were failing as we looked in vain for help. We watched from our towers for a nation that could not save us." (Lamentations 4:17). They watched for help that couldn't save them. I think that's a heavy thing to read.

The poet says, "Those who chased us were swifter than the eagles in the sky…" (Lamentations 4:19). An eagle moves fast, and these pursuers were swifter. They pursued the people over the mountains and ambushed them in the wilderness.

Gazelles are fast, but that's not the animal he picks. The poet says the ones who chased them "…were swifter than the eagles in the sky…" (Lamentations 4:19). He looks up to the sky, not to a field. Then he adds that they pursued them over the mountains.

The mountains do show up, but not with deer. The poet says, "Those who chased us were swifter than the eagles in the sky; they pursued us over the mountains and ambushed us in the wilderness." (Lamentations 4:19). The animal he names is the eagle, and the pursuers were swifter than that.

explanations.answer: They would live under his shadow
explanations.explanation: The poet says, "We had said of him, “Under his shadow we will live among the nations.”" (Lamentations 4:20). They counted on the LORD's anointed to cover them. Then he was captured in their pits. That's a hard fall for a hope.

explanations.answer: He would rebuild the temple walls
explanations.explanation: Rebuilding isn't what the people said. The poet says they had said of him, "Under his shadow we will live among the nations." (Lamentations 4:20). They counted on his shadow to cover them. Then he was captured in their pits.

explanations.answer: He would make them rich again
explanations.explanation: Riches aren't part of it. The poet says they had said, "Under his shadow we will live among the nations." (Lamentations 4:20). They spoke of living under his shadow, not of money. Then he was captured in their pits.

explanations.answer: She will get drunk and expose herself
explanations.explanation: The poet says, "Yet the cup will pass to you as well; you will get drunk and expose yourself." (Lamentations 4:21). The Daughter of Edom is told to rejoice and be glad. Yet the cup will pass to her too.

explanations.answer: She will share it with her allies
explanations.explanation: Nothing is said about allies. The poet says, "…the cup will pass to you as well; you will get drunk and expose yourself." (Lamentations 4:21). The cup comes to her. Rejoicing now doesn't skip her.

explanations.answer: She will pour it out on the ground
explanations.explanation: She doesn't get to pour it out. The poet says, "…the cup will pass to you as well; you will get drunk and expose yourself." (Lamentations 4:21). She drinks it, and that's what comes of it. The cup reaches her, friend.

The poet says, "O Daughter of Zion, your punishment is complete; He will not prolong your exile." (Lamentations 4:22). After all the dark verses, here's a word of hope. The punishment is complete. The exile won't be stretched out.

The poet actually says it is complete. He says, "O Daughter of Zion, your punishment is complete; He will not prolong your exile." (Lamentations 4:22). So the dark isn't the last word for her. The exile won't be stretched out.

The poet says the opposite for Edom. He says, "But He will punish your iniquity, O Daughter of Edom; He will expose your sins." (Lamentations 4:22). Her iniquity doesn't go unpunished. The poem ends with the promise that Zion's exile won't be prolonged and Edom's sins will be exposed.

Right. The poet says, "But He will punish your iniquity, O Daughter of Edom; He will expose your sins." (Lamentations 4:22). So Edom's rejoicing won't be the end of her story. It's a sobering way to end the poem.
